name: Lipmaxxing

lead: Lipmaxxing groups together the things people do to make their lips look fuller, smoother and better defined. Forum guides describe lips as one of the features that shape how the lower face and smile read, and they frame fuller, well-hydrated lips as looking more youthful.

The methods range from daily lip care (moisturising, balms, hyaluronic acid serums, brushing) through temporary plumping products and tints to clinic procedures such as hyaluronic acid filler or fat transfer. Medical literature describes the clinic procedures; the at-home routines are discussed mainly on forums.

paras: Forum guides describe a routine of hydrating the lips with balm or petroleum jelly, using a hyaluronic acid serum or moisturiser, and sometimes brushing the lips. Some users report that brushing swells the lips for a short time only. Others get filler from a licensed injector. Tints and lip colour are used to change the apparent shape and colour.

Dermatology and surgical sources list redness, swelling, bruising and itching after fillers, with lumps, unevenness and an overfilled appearance also possible. Permanent filler materials have caused nodules requiring removal. Irritant plumpers cause temporary swelling by irritating the lips. Fillers are procedures for a qualified practitioner, and people with certain conditions are advised against them.

angle.text: Hydration and tints change how the lips look right away, while fillers or fat transfer add volume for months or longer. Practitioners use these to change lip size, shape and colour.

lead: Lipmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for improving the size, shape, hydration and colour of the lips. Community guides present lips as part of the lower-face and smile area and describe fuller lips as looking more youthful and giving a more appealing smile.[1]

The same guides break lip fullness down into collagen and hyaluronic acid levels in the lip tissue, stored fat, hydration, and age and hormones, and note that dry, cracked lips can look smaller and deflated, which is why moisturising is a staple of the approach.[1] Approaches range from topical care and tints to clinic procedures: a general overview of lip augmentation lists hyaluronic acid and other injectable fillers, fat transfer, implants, and temporary non-surgical plumpers and suction devices.[2]

Research on the clinic side includes rating studies in which observers scored photographs of lips before and after hyaluronic acid filler, with results that depend on starting lip fullness, and regulators such as the US FDA treat fillers as medical devices to be injected by licensed practitioners.[3][4][5] Home routines such as brushing are discussed mainly on forums, and no published trial tests them.[6]

Lip lift, lip filler, 'trout pout', 'filler transparency' [2][11]

paras: Forum guides list the factors behind lip fullness as collagen and hyaluronic acid content, fat stored in the lips, hydration, and age and hormones. They say estrogen can increase blood flow and swelling in the lips, and that lips thin with age as fat and collagen decline.[1]

Lipmaxxing therefore covers both maintenance (keeping lips moist and supple) and enhancement (adding volume or changing colour). Clinical sources define lip augmentation as using fillers or implants to increase lip size, correct asymmetry, add protrusion or change the balance between the upper and lower lips.[2]

Users describe moisturising, using petroleum jelly to prevent chapping, applying hyaluronic acid serum, and lip brushing. On looksmax.org one user says brushing makes lips look bigger for about a minute through swelling, while another asks what brushing is meant to do, showing the technique is not universally understood or agreed on.[6]

Lip balms form an occlusive layer that seals in moisture; common ingredients include beeswax, carnauba wax, petroleum jelly and lanolin.[7] A 2015 study funded by a balm manufacturer, in 32 women, reported hydration lasting about eight hours after application and improved barrier function.[7] Wikipedia also records that some physicians have suggested certain balms cause dependence, while manufacturers deny this and professionals disagree, and that scented or flavoured balms can irritate sensitive lips.[7]
Lip plumpers contain irritants such as capsaicin that cause temporary swelling, and suction pumps draw blood into the lips for temporary fullness.[2]

Hyaluronic acid is among the most common filler materials because it occurs naturally in the body and is biodegradable; most products are cross-linked with BDDE for stability and longer duration.[8] Wikipedia describes Restylane as a non-animal hyaluronic acid gel that usually lasts about six months, and Juvederm as containing about 35 percent more cross-linked hyaluronic acid and claimed to last up to 1 to 1.5 years.[2] An aesthetics practitioner interviewed in 2021 put properly administered fillers at 6 to 15 months.[9]

The FDA states that certain fillers are approved for adults aged 22 and older to add volume to the lips, cheeks, chin and back of the hand, with approval depending on the specific product.[5] The agency advises that filler injection be treated as a medical procedure performed by a licensed provider trained in filler injection.[5]

subs.h: Fat transfer, implants and other materials
paras: Fat transfer, in which fat harvested from elsewhere on the body is injected or placed in the lips, is described as one of the best options for semi-permanent results, though it can cause lumps or scarring.[2] Implants include ePTFE (Gore-Tex) strips and tubes.[2] Permanent PMMA microsphere fillers have caused nodules near the lip edges, and some cases required surgical removal.[2] Surgical lip augmentation by moving skin flaps adds little volume.[2]

Hyaluronidase, an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, is injected to dissolve hyaluronic acid fillers and to treat complications, and Wikipedia calls it the best option for dissolving lip filler.[10] The 2023 Refinery29 feature reported that the same enzyme can also break down natural hyaluronic acid, and that some people felt they looked worse afterwards.[11]

Early attempts at lip augmentation included paraffin injections around 1900, described as unsuccessful, and liquid silicone from the early 1960s, abandoned about thirty years later over health and long-term appearance concerns.[2] Injectable bovine collagen became the benchmark around 1980; it lasted about four weeks to three months and required an allergy test.[2]

More materials arrived in the late 1990s as cosmetic surgery grew, and since about 2000 very fine needles (30 to 31 gauge) and topical anaesthetic have made hyaluronic acid injections more comfortable.[2] The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported 778,000 Restylane procedures in 2006.[2]

A 2019 study in Archives of Plastic Surgery had 217 observers rate 15 women's lower-face photographs in natural, simulated upper-lip-filler and simulated upper-lip-lift versions. Natural photos scored highest for attractiveness, perceived success and perceived health, filler scored above the lift, and the differences were statistically significant but small; images were simulated and most observers were educated white women from the Midwest.[4]

A 2023 Scientific Reports study compared before and about ten-day-after photographs of 16 women treated with hyaluronic acid filler, rated by 327 evaluators (laypersons, general dentists and facial aesthetics specialists). In the thinner-lip group the mean attractiveness score rose from 3.89 to 4.74, while in the thicker-lip group it fell from 6.38 to 5.82; laypersons scored lower than dentists and specialists, and the authors concluded filler amounts should be individualised.[3]

Common effects after filler injection are redness, swelling, itching and bruising, usually fading within a week; lumps, ridges and unevenness can also occur.[2] Overfilling can produce an exaggerated look sometimes called a trout pout.[2] The FDA lists less common effects as nodules, infection, sores, allergic reactions and tissue death, and rare serious ones including filler migration, permanent hard nodules, and injection into a blood vessel that can cause tissue death, vision problems including blindness, or stroke; some effects can appear months or years later.[5] Wikipedia lists people who may be advised against lip filler, including those with lidocaine allergy, active cold sores, clotting disorders, infection, lupus or severe hypertension, and notes that smoking slows healing.[2]

The FDA says it has not approved over-the-counter fillers, needle-free injection devices or injectable silicone for aesthetic use, and asks that patients not inject themselves or buy fillers online because products may be counterfeit or unapproved.[5] In October 2021 Good Morning America reported on needle-free 'hyaluron pens' sold online for as little as $40 and popularised on TikTok, with a New York aesthetics practitioner describing severe bruising, lumps and tissue damage in patients treated with them.[9]

Refinery29's 2023 feature described a 'filler transparency' trend in which TikTok and Instagram creators film their own lip filler appointments; dermatologist Corey Hartman was quoted as saying lips are now the new gateway to cosmetic treatment rather than Botox.[11] Plastic surgeons told the outlet that younger people increasingly treat filler casually, and one physician coined the term 'perception drift' for procedures changing how people see their own faces.[11] The same piece recorded public figures such as Ariana Grande, who said she stopped lip filler in 2018, and Courteney Cox, who had filler dissolved in 2017.[11]
On looksmax.org lipmaxxing is grouped with other lower-face and style topics, and guides mix hydration advice, product questions and clinic filler.[1][6]

No studies found of home lipmaxxing routines such as brushing. Rating studies of hyaluronic acid filler and simulated lip changes exist and are described above, and the wider medical literature on lip augmentation is summarised in general references.[3][4][2]

lore.intro: Lipmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix routines, product questions and debate about which methods are worthwhile.[1][6]

claims.claim: Full lips look more youthful and make a smile more appealing
Hyaluronic acid and hydration improve lip fullness

Filler can be fully reversed if you do not like it

timeline.event: Paraffin injections for lip augmentation are described as unsuccessful.[2]
Liquid silicone is used for augmentation and is abandoned around thirty years later over health concerns.[2]
Bovine collagen is introduced and becomes the comparison standard for later fillers.[2]
Fine 30 to 31 gauge needles, topical anaesthetic and hyaluronic acid gels such as Restylane and Juvederm make filler a mainstream option.[2]
The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reports 778,000 Restylane procedures.[2]
Actress Courteney Cox has her filler dissolved, an early celebrity example of reversal.[11]
Ariana Grande says she stopped lip filler and Botox.[11]
Archives of Plastic Surgery publishes a rating study of simulated upper-lip filler and lip lift.[4]
The FDA warns about needle-free hyaluron pens as the devices spread on TikTok.[9]
Scientific Reports publishes a study of lip attractiveness before and after hyaluronic acid filler in thin and thick lips.[3]
